text: Highly polarizable solvents enable adaptive electrolytes for practical lithium–sulfur batteries Shang Shi , Wanyu Zhao , Zhengqing Fan , Keying Guo , Jiayi Li , Zhan Gao , Qinghua Meng , Xiaowei Yang * School of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering, State Key Laboratory of Synergistic Chem–Bio Synthesis, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai 200240, China A R T I C L E I N F O Keywords: Lithium-sulfur batteries High polarizability solvents Adaptive electrolytes Force matching Charge-density-dependent solvation A B S T R A C T In lithium-sulfur (Li-S) batteries, the charge density variation of Sn 2- results in fluctuating ionic bonds in lithium polysulfides (Li2Sn), and its mismatch with conventional electrolytes’ fixed solvating force lead to challenges in optimizing polysulfide shuttling and sluggish reaction kinetics simultaneously.
Therefore, designing electrolytes capable of adaptively adjusting solvating forces in response to changes in the electrostatic interactions of Li2Sn is imperative for practical Li-S batteries.

Herein, we propose an electrostatic interaction force matching concept that utilize high polarizability solvents with dynamical solvating power to accommodate the fluctuation in electrostatic interactions of Li2Sn.

Molecules with conjugated structure exhibit significantly delocalized electron cloud, which is capable of responding in real time to the stimulus of local-electric-field variations from Sn 2– to enable charge–density–dependent solvation regulation of Li2Sn.

Weakly or strongly polarized solvents induced by Sn 2– with different charge–density reduce the solubility of long-chain Li2Sn (n > 4) by over 50% and enable a magnitude-level increase in the solubility of short-chain Li2Sn (n ≤4), promoting the reaction kinetic and pre­ venting the accumulation of Li2Sn.
Consequently, optimized Li–S batteries achieve 406.2 Wh/kg in 3 Ah–level pouch cells with E/S ratio of 3 mL/gsulfur.
The findings deepen the understanding of polarizable systems and provide an innovative electrolyte design principle. 1.
Introduction The escalating energy crisis and environmental challenges have sparked unprecedented interest in renewable energy and efficient en­ ergy storage technologies.

Among emerging solutions, Li–S batteries stand out due to their remarkable theoretical energy density of 2600 Wh/kg and abundant raw material reserves, positioning them as a promising next–generation energy storage system [1–4].
However, their practical energy density and cycling stability are severely restricted by sluggish reactions kinetics and shuttle effect, especially at lean electro­ lyte conditions [5–7].
It has been demonstrated that regulations of electrolyte solvating forces have the capacity of optimizing the solvation and reactivity of Li2Sn and addressing above issues [8–10].

Conventional electrolytes with strong solvating forces can enhance the dispersion of short-chain Li2Sn with strong electrostatic interactions and improve re­ action kinetics, while those with weak solvating forces can confine the long-chain Li2Sn, which are prone to diffusion, on the cathode side to prevent shuttling [11–14].

Although these conventional electrolytes can address part issues in Li-S batteries, their solvating forces fail to adapt to the variations in electrostatic interactions of Li2Sn and achieve force-matching with all Li2Sn, which may exacerbate other issues: highly solvating electrolytes exacerbate the Li2Sn shuttle effect, while sparingly solvating electrolytes aggravate the sluggish reaction kinetics.
It’s difficult for conventional electrolytes to simultaneously ensure the cycling stability and the improvement of energy density of Li-S batteries [19–21].

Therefore, designing electrolytes that can both enhance reaction kinetics and suppress the shuttle effect is imperative for the practical application of Li–S batteries and remains substantia challenges.

Detailed analysis of the properties of Li2Sn is essential to elucidate the fundamental reasons behind the bidirectional regulation re­ quirements and design electrolytes that address the inherent contra­ dictions in Li–S batteries.

The fixed solvating forces of electrolyte and bidirectional regulation requirements for solvating forces of electrolyte dictated by the dynamic changes in the charge density of Sn 2– result in distinct sol­ vation microenvironments for different Li2Sn, in which the degree of solvation and reactivities of Li2Sn differ significantly and lead to the contradiction between shuttle suppression and kinetic optimization.

Therefore, the electrolytes exhibiting adaptive solvating capabilities toward different Li2Sn, thereby simultaneously reducing the solubility of long-chain Li2Sn while enhancing that of short-chain Li2Sn could resolve this intrinsic and fundamental contradiction in Li-S batteries.

However, there are few reports on the electrolytes capable of dynamically adjusting their solvating forces in response to the charge density varia­ tions of Sn 2– and enabling rapid reactions free from shuttle effect to comprehensively enhance the performance of Li–S batteries.

In this work, we propose an electrostatic interaction force matching concept that leverages the Sn 2––charge–density–dependent ion–dipole interaction between Li2Sn and high polarizability solvent molecules to achieve selective solvation and stable dispersion of various Li2Sn.

The solvent molecules with high electronic polarizability are capable of undergoing electronic rearrangement in response to the local electro­ static field of Sn 2– across different chain lengths, and the degree of po­ larization and dipole charge density depend on the charge density of Sn 2– [27].

Considering the electron cloud of the solvent must exhibit strong elasticity and compatibility with lithium metal, we employed N, N-Dimethyltrifluoromethanesulfonamide (DMTMSA) as model solvent, which incorporates a sulfonamide group—highly polarizable moiety with conjugated structure and resonant modes that exhibit significantly delocalized electron cloud, making it more sensitive to the changes in electrostatic field intensity of Sn 2– (Fig.

Low charge–density Sn 2– induce only minimal polarization of DMTMSA, resulting in weak ion­ –dipole interactions with long–chain Li2Sn and sparingly solvating, whereas high charge–density Sn 2– exhibits the opposite situation, and strong ion–dipole interactions are established between DMTMSA and short–chain Li2Sn, achieving highly solvating [28–30].

Based on this mechanism, DMTMSA enables adaptive adjustment of solvating forces based on the charge density of Sn 2– within different Li2Sn solvation mi­ croenvironments, reducing the solubility of long-chain Li2Sn by over 50% and enable a magnitude-level increase in the solubility of short-chain Li2Sn (Fig.

This not only effectively suppressed the shuttle effect but also enhanced the reaction kinetic without posing new issues, and the optimized reaction kinetic enable three–dimensional deposition of Li2S, preventing rapid coverage of cathode active sites (Fig. 1b)[31].
Consequently, practical applicability is demonstrated in 3 Ah–level Li–S pouch cells with an actual energy density of 406.2 Wh/kg with E/S = 3 mL/gs.

Moreover, we validate the mechanism's universality by applying it to solvents exhibiting similar tautomeric equilibria (e.g., amide molecules), offering a transformative approach to electrolyte design for Li–S batteries. 2.

In detail, the Li–S bat­ tery was subjected to 15 min charge/discharge cycles to induce polari­ zation, followed by a 2 h rest period to allow the system to return to thermodynamic equilibrium.
According to the Butler–Volmer equation and Ohm's law, the instantaneous drop to zero upon current interruption corresponds to ohmic and activation polarization.
Ohmic polarization is calculated as the product of Rohm and the test current based on Ohm's law.
By subtracting the ohmic polarization component, the activation polarization value can be determined.
In contrast, concentration polar­ ization, governed by the Nernst–Planck equation, persists due to the time–delayed nature of mass transport and gradually diminishes during relaxation.
This method enables precise differentiation and quantitative analysis of the three types of polarization, which is the primary element influencing reaction kinetics.

The results indicate that both the DMTMSA battery and the control battery exhibit three distinct stages of concentration polarization during discharge, and these stages roughly correspond to the depth of discharge (DOD) ranges of 0~0.3, 0.3~0.9, and 0.9~1.0 (Fig. 4a).

The discharge curves reveal that during the DOD range of 0~0.3, the primary reaction is the reduction of Li2S8 to Li2S4, and the concentration polarization in this stage is mainly caused by the slow diffusion of Li2S8 from the bulk electrolyte to the electrode surface, with negligible differences observed between DMTMSA batteries and control batteries (Fig.
However, near DOD ≈0.3, a sharp increase in concentration polarization occurs, and the dominant reaction shifts to the reduction of Li2S4 to Li2S.
Here, the polarization is primarily governed by the sluggish diffusion of Li2S4.

Notably, the DMTMSA batteries exhibit significantly lower polarization than the control group, demonstrating DMTMSA's role in enhancing the solubility and dispersion of Li2S4 and achieving Li2S three–dimensional growth.
The further intensification of concentration polarization in the third stage may be attributed to the depletion of Li2S4.
The activation polarization, which stems from sluggish interfacial charge transfer processes, exhibits a stepwise variation pattern similar to that of concentration polarization.
DMTMSA batteries generally exhibit lower activation polarization compared to control batteries, which aligns with the data obtained from CV and EIS measurements (Fig. 4b).
During the DOD range of 0~0.3, the variation in activation polarization of both DMTMSA battery and control battery is minimal, as evidenced by the nearly horizontal lines in the data plot.
Once the DOD exceeds 0.3, the gap in activation polarization between the DMTMSA battery and the control battery widens significantly.
The DMTMSA battery shows minimal increase in activation polarization, whereas the control battery exhibits an accelerating growth rate as DOD increases.
It is noteworthy that the activation polarization of the control group gradually increased, and the nucleation of Li2S covering the cathode surface continued to adversely affect the reaction.

Discussions on Figure S31.
From the results shown in Figure S31, it can be observed that DMTMSA does not exert its maximum effect at lower concentrations.
Conversely, when the content is excessively high, the solubility of Li2S8 becomes too low, causing the conversion to favor a quasi-solid-state form.
This excessive suppression of the liquid-phase-mediated pathway is detrimental to battery performance.
Therefore, there exists an optimal moderate concentration for DMTMSA.
